attributes.body:
In Japanese, い-Adjectives are known as 'form containing words', and are used to describe nouns. All い-Adjectives end in い in their base form.

As mentioned, all い-Adjectives end in い in their base form. However, not all words ending in い are い-Adjectives. Let's take a look at some of the words that are commonly mistaken for い-Adjectives.

In addition to きらい above, there is also きれい. きれい actually comes from the kanji structure 綺麗（きれい）, with い being part of the kanji itself. This is never the case with い-Adjectives, where the い will always be outside of the kanji. Due to the kanji for 綺麗（きれい） being somewhat difficult, this word is often written in hiragana or katakana, which leads to confusion for learners. Unfortunately there is no rule for distinguishing which words ending in い are not い-Adjectives, but thankfully, there are not very many of them, so it won't be long before you become familiar with them.

Caution

Unlike な-Adjectives, い-Adjectives must never be followed by だ. This is due to だ only being able to conjugate with nouns (which な-Adjectives originally are). Instead, です is used with い-Adjectives to make them sound more polite.

Fun Fact

Although using です with い-Adjectives is very common, it is actually incorrect Japanese. As です is simply a polite variation of だ, it follows all of the same conjugation rules as だ. This means that it should only be attached to nouns and な-Adjectives. However, as most Japanese natives do not know this rule, it is widely considered natural to use.

attributes.source: [DBJG] A Dictionary of Basic Japanese Grammar

attributes.body: い-Adjectives describe qualities or states. They can modify nouns (e.g., 暑い日 = 'hot day') or end a sentence (e.g., 今日は暑い = 'Today is hot'). いい ('good') is an い-adjective, but it's irregular—it becomes よく when used with verbs, unlike most い-adjectives which don't change their base form.

い-Adjectives describe the state or characteristics of nouns and can be used at the end of a sentence or directly before a noun. For example, 面白い本 means 'an interesting book.' Similarly, Japanese verbs, unlike English verbs, can also modify nouns. For example, 読んだ本 means 'the book [I] read.'

い-Adjectives attach directly to nouns (e.g., 面白い本) and don't use だ in plain form (e.g., この本は面白い). な-Adjectives attach to nouns with な (e.g., 好きな本) and do use だ in plain form (e.g., この本は好きだ). Note that not all adjectives ending in い are い-Adjectives—for example, きれい (綺麗) ends in い but is a な-Adjective, as in きれいな月.

い-Adjectives describe the state or appearance of nouns, like 白いドレス ('a white dress'). They can also form the predicate, describing the main topic of a sentence. For example, 今日は暑い means 'Today is hot.' Unlike English, an い-Adjective can stand alone as a complete sentence (e.g., 暑い means 'It's hot' without needing an equivalent of 'it').
